warmup.q: sealed class Fee permits Flat, Percent {} is not abstract, and Flat and Percent are its final subclasses. A switch expression over a Fee has case Flat f and case Percent p and no default. Does it compile?
options: Yes: the permits list is complete, so the switch is exhaustive
No: new Fee() is also a possible value, so the switch misses a case
No: only interfaces can be sealed
Yes, but a plain Fee throws MatchException at run time
warmup.why: A concrete sealed class can be instantiated itself, so a Fee that is neither Flat nor Percent can exist, and javac reports the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. Make Fee abstract, or an interface, and the two cases cover it. Kotlin sidesteps the trap: a sealed class there is always abstract.

sections.h: A sealed type closes the list of direct subtypes
sections.html:
An interface normally says nothing about who implements it. Add sealed and a permits clause, and the list of implementations becomes part of the type:

Java
public sealed interface Command permits Authorize, Capture, Refund {}

public record Authorize(String authCode, long amountMinor) implements Command {}
public record Capture() implements Command {}
public record Refund(long amountMinor) implements Command {}
Kotlin
sealed interface Command {
    data class Authorize(val authCode: String, val amountMinor: Long) : Command
    data object Capture : Command
    data class Refund(val amountMinor: Long) : Command
}

Sealed classes and interfaces have been final since JDK 17 (JEP 409). javac checks the list from both sides. A class that implements Command without being on it fails with class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Command (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause). javac also writes the list into the class file as a PermittedSubclasses attribute, and the JVM checks it when it loads a class. A subclass compiled against an older, unsealed Command fails to load with IncompatibleClassChangeError: class Void cannot implement sealed interface Command.

You can leave permits out when every subtype is declared in the same source file as the sealed type. javac then takes the subtypes it finds there. Reflection shows the result: Command.class.isSealed() is true, and getPermittedSubclasses() returns the three records.

Kotlin has no permits clause. Its rule is location: any class in the same package and the same module may extend a sealed type, and a class anywhere else fails with a class can only extend a sealed class or interface declared in the same package. With the JDK 21 target these labs use, kotlinc 2.4 writes the same PermittedSubclasses attribute as javac. So Java code sees a Kotlin sealed interface as sealed: a Java switch over it needs no default, and javac rejects a Java class that tries to implement it.

Sealing restricts direct subtypes only. Refund.class.isSealed() is false, and what happens below each permitted subtype is the subject of the next section.

try.title: Break the list on purpose
steps: Run SealedBasics (or SealedBasicsKt) with the command below.
In the Java demo, uncomment static final class Void implements Command {} and run again. Read the error.
Add Void to the permits clause and delete final from it. Run again. Then put final back.
Now delete the whole permits ... clause and run. What does getPermittedSubclasses() print?
In the Kotlin twin, uncomment class Void : Command. Does it compile? Why is that different from Java?

code.title: SealedBasics.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Modifier; /** A sealed interface names its direct subtypes, and the JVM keeps that list. */ public class SealedBasics { sealed interface Command permits Authorize, Capture, Refund {} record Authorize(String authCode, long amountMinor) implements Command {} // records are final record Capture() implements Command {} record Refund(long amountMinor) implements Command {} // Step 2: uncomment this line and compile. // static final class Void implements Command {} public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Command.isSealed(): " + Command.class.isSealed()); for (Class<?> c : Command.class.getPermittedSubclasses()) { System.out.println("permits: " + c.getSimpleName() + (Modifier.isFinal(c.getModifiers()) ? " (final)" : "")); } System.out.println("Refund.isSealed(): " + Refund.class.isSealed()); } }

alt.title: SealedBasics.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo import java.lang.reflect.Modifier // Kotlin has no permits clause: the direct subtypes are the ones declared in this package and module sealed interface Command { data class Authorize(val authCode: String, val amountMinor: Long) : Command // final by default data object Capture : Command data class Refund(val amountMinor: Long) : Command } // Step 2: uncomment this line and compile. Then try it in another package. // class Void : Command /** kotlinc writes the same PermittedSubclasses attribute that javac does. */ fun main() { println("Command.isSealed(): ${Command::class.java.isSealed}") for (c in Command::class.java.permittedSubclasses) { println("permits: ${c.simpleName}" + if (Modifier.isFinal(c.modifiers)) " (final)" else "") } println("Refund.isSealed(): ${Command.Refund::class.java.isSealed}") }

try.expect: The first run prints isSealed(): true, the three records marked (final), and Refund.isSealed(): false. The unlisted class fails with class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Command (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause). Listed but without a modifier, it fails with sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected. With no permits clause, javac infers all four from the file and prints Void too. In Kotlin, class Void : Command compiles: the list is whatever sits in the same package and module.

sections.h: final, sealed or non-sealed: every branch has to choose
sections.html:
Every permitted subtype of a sealed type must say how its own branch ends, with exactly one of three modifiers. If a class says nothing, javac stops with sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected. An interface can't be final, so for one the message is sealed or non-sealed modifiers expected.

final ends the branch. Records and enums are implicitly final, so a record needs no modifier, which is one reason sealed interfaces and records fit together so well. sealed continues the closed list one level down, with its own permits. non-sealed reopens the branch on purpose: anyone may extend it, in any package.

Java
public sealed interface PaymentMethod permits Card, BankTransfer, PartnerMethod {}
public record Card(String network) implements PaymentMethod {}                      // final
public sealed interface BankTransfer extends PaymentMethod permits Sepa, Swift {}   // closed below
public non-sealed interface PartnerMethod extends PaymentMethod {                   // open below
    String partnerId();
}
Kotlin
sealed interface PaymentMethod {
    data class Card(val network: String) : PaymentMethod                             // final by default
    sealed interface BankTransfer : PaymentMethod                                     // closed below
    interface PartnerMethod : PaymentMethod { val partnerId: String }                 // open below
}

non-sealed sounds like it defeats the point of sealing. It doesn't, because the compiler still knows the shape of the tree. A switch covers the open branch with one case PartnerMethod p, and that case matches every partner class, including ones a partner team writes next year. Your switch stays exhaustive and the partner team stays free. Kotlin has no non-sealed keyword: a plain interface or an open class under a sealed parent plays the same role.

So "sealed means final" is wrong: a sealed type has subtypes by definition, and a non-sealed branch can have any number. The trap that catches people in code review is a third one. A sealed class that isn't abstract is itself a possible value. With sealed class Fee permits Flat, Percent and no abstract, new Fee() is legal, so a switch with cases for Flat and Percent fails with the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. Make the parent abstract, or make it an interface. Kotlin avoids the trap entirely: its docs say a sealed class is always abstract.

try.title: Reopen one branch, close the trap
steps: Run NonSealedDemo. GiftCard is partner code: which modifier lets it exist?
Delete non-sealed from PartnerMethod, leaving a plain interface, and run. Read the error, then put it back.
Delete abstract from sealed abstract static class Fee and run again.

code.title: NonSealedDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo; /** Each branch of a sealed hierarchy ends as final, sealed or non-sealed. */ public class NonSealedDemo { sealed interface PaymentMethod permits Card, BankTransfer, PartnerMethod {} record Card(String network) implements PaymentMethod {} // final: a leaf sealed interface BankTransfer extends PaymentMethod permits Sepa, Swift {} // sealed: closed below record Sepa(String iban) implements BankTransfer {} record Swift(String bic) implements BankTransfer {} non-sealed interface PartnerMethod extends PaymentMethod { // non-sealed: open below String partnerId(); } // partner code: allowed, because PartnerMethod is non-sealed record GiftCard(String partnerId, String code) implements PartnerMethod {} // Step 3: delete "abstract" here and compile. sealed abstract static class Fee permits Flat, Percent {} static final class Flat extends Fee { final long minor; Flat(long minor) { this.minor = minor; } } static final class Percent extends Fee { final int basisPoints; Percent(int basisPoints) { this.basisPoints = basisPoints; } } static String describe(PaymentMethod m) { return switch (m) { case Card c -> "card " + c.network(); case BankTransfer t -> "bank transfer " + t; // one case for the sealed branch case PartnerMethod p -> "partner " + p.partnerId(); // one case for the open branch }; } static long fee(Fee f, long amountMinor) { return switch (f) { case Flat flat -> flat.minor; case Percent pct -> amountMinor * pct.basisPoints / 10_000; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(describe(new Card("VISA"))); System.out.println(describe(new Sepa("DE89370400440532013000"))); System.out.println(describe(new GiftCard("giftly", "GC-7731"))); System.out.println("PartnerMethod.isSealed(): " + PartnerMethod.class.isSealed()); System.out.println("fee: " + fee(new Percent(290), 10_000) + " and " + fee(new Flat(35), 10_000)); } }

alt.title: NonSealedDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo // Kotlin subtypes are final unless you open them, and there is no non-sealed keyword: // a plain interface (or an open class) under a sealed parent is the open branch. sealed interface PaymentMethod { data class Card(val network: String) : PaymentMethod // final: a leaf sealed interface BankTransfer : PaymentMethod // sealed: closed below data class Sepa(val iban: String) : BankTransfer data class Swift(val bic: String) : BankTransfer interface PartnerMethod : PaymentMethod { // open below val partnerId: String } } // partner code, which could live in any package: PartnerMethod is an ordinary interface data class GiftCard(override val partnerId: String, val code: String) : PaymentMethod.PartnerMethod // A Kotlin sealed class is always abstract, so the trap in step 3 of the Java demo can't happen here. sealed class Fee { class Flat(val minor: Long) : Fee() class Percent(val basisPoints: Int) : Fee() } fun describe(m: PaymentMethod): String = when (m) { is PaymentMethod.Card -> "card ${m.network}" is PaymentMethod.BankTransfer -> "bank transfer $m" // one branch for the sealed branch is PaymentMethod.PartnerMethod -> "partner ${m.partnerId}" // one branch for the open branch } fun fee(f: Fee, amountMinor: Long): Long = when (f) { is Fee.Flat -> f.minor is Fee.Percent -> amountMinor * f.basisPoints / 10_000 } /** Each branch of a sealed hierarchy ends closed, sealed again, or open. */ fun main() { println(describe(PaymentMethod.Card("VISA"))) println(describe(PaymentMethod.Sepa("DE89370400440532013000"))) println(describe(GiftCard("giftly", "GC-7731"))) println("PartnerMethod.isSealed(): ${PaymentMethod.PartnerMethod::class.java.isSealed}") println("fee: ${fee(Fee.Percent(290), 10_000)} and ${fee(Fee.Flat(35), 10_000)}") }

Without a modifier, javac says sealed or non-sealed modifiers expected (an interface can't be final, so final isn't offered). Without abstract, the fee switch fails with the switch expression does not cover all possible input values: a plain Fee is now a possible value. The Kotlin twin can't show that trap, because its sealed class is always abstract.

sections.html:
Sealing ties a hierarchy to one place, and Java and Kotlin draw the boundary slightly differently.

In Java the permitted subtypes must be in the same module as the sealed type. If your code isn't in a named module, they must be in the same package. A typical Quarkus or Spring service runs on the class path, in the unnamed module, so the package rule is the one you will meet. Split a sealed interface and its record across pay.api and pay.card and javac refuses:

error: class PaymentMethod in unnamed module cannot extend a sealed class in a different package
public sealed interface PaymentMethod permits pay.card.Card {}

The wording is clumsy, since it names the sealed interface as the class doing the extending, but the rule is clear. Add a module-info.java that puts both packages in one module, and the same files compile.

Kotlin's rule is the same package and the same module, whether or not you use JPMS modules. So for the code most of us write, the two languages agree: keep a sealed hierarchy in one package. That is rarely a burden. The subtypes are usually small records or data classes that read best next to each other, often nested inside the sealed type itself, which also lets Java infer permits.

The restriction makes sense once you see what sealing promises. The author of a sealed type says "this is the complete list", and the compiler can only hold everyone to that if the whole list is compiled and shipped as one unit. A subtype in some other module could be released on its own schedule, and the list every switch was checked against would quietly go stale.

try.title: Split a hierarchy across packages
steps: The folder labs/modernjava/javac/sealed-packages holds a sealed PaymentMethod in pay.api, a Card record in pay.card, and a module-info.java. Gradle doesn't compile it; you run javac yourself.
Run the first command. Read the error and the line it points at.
Run the second command, which adds the module descriptor.
Predict, then check: move Card.java into pay/api/, change its package line to pay.api, change the permits clause to permits Card, and run the first command again.

code.title: terminal
code.html: cd labs/modernjava/javac/sealed-packages # 1. class path, unnamed module: two packages are not allowed javac -d ../../build/sealed-packages pay/api/PaymentMethod.java pay/card/Card.java # 2. one named module: two packages are fine javac -d ../../build/sealed-packages module-info.java pay/api/PaymentMethod.java pay/card/Card.java

The second compiles with no output, because both packages belong to module pay. After the move, the first command compiles too: on the class path, one package is enough.

sections.h: Let the compiler find every switch, and keep default out
sections.html:
Sealing pays off in a switch. Over a sealed type, javac knows every possible subtype, so a switch with one case per subtype needs no default, and javac checks that the cases really cover every subtype:

Java
static long ledgerImpact(Dispute d) {
    return switch (d) {                            // no default
        case Opened o -> -o.amountMinor();
        case EvidenceSent e -> 0;
        case Won w -> 0;
        case Lost l -> -l.amountMinor();
    };
}
Kotlin
fun ledgerImpact(d: Dispute): Long = when (d) {    // no else
    is Dispute.Opened -> -d.amountMinor
    is Dispute.EvidenceSent -> 0
    is Dispute.Won -> 0
    is Dispute.Lost -> -d.amountMinor
}

Now the card schemes add an arbitration stage, and you add Arbitration to Dispute. Every switch over Dispute without a default stops compiling. On JDK 21 to 26 the error is the bare the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, pointing at the switch. JDK 27 adds the cases you're missing:

error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values
        return switch (d) {
               ^
  missing patterns:
      Arbitration _

kotlinc has always been specific: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Arbitration' branch or an 'else' branch. Either way, the build hands you the list of code to update.

A default throws that list away. It means "and anything else", so Arbitration drops into it without a word and gets whatever the default returns. The OpenJDK team's 2026 guide to switching over sealed types has a section titled "By default, avoid default", because a default "sweeps errors, both present and future, under the rug". Use default only where you really mean "everything else", such as the illegal (state, event) pairs in a state machine, as State and Chain of Responsibility in the patterns track did.

The same guide asks authors to say in the Javadoc why a type is sealed. It names two reasons: the type models a closed domain, like dispute stages, or the author only wants to control who implements it. Say which, and whether you expect to add subtypes, so the people switching over it know what to expect. Exhaustive also doesn't mean unbreakable at run time: a client compiled against the old list can still meet an Arbitration from a newer jar. Lesson 3 shows what happens then.

try.title: Add a stage to the dispute flow
steps: Run DisputeSwitches once and look at the three functions: label, ledgerImpact and slaDays. Which one has a default?
Add Arbitration to the permits clause and uncomment the Arbitration record. Before you run, predict which functions javac will report.
Run it, then make it compile again by handling Arbitration where javac asked. What does slaDays return for an arbitration case now? Is that right?
Do the same in the Kotlin twin, DisputeSwitchesKt.

code.title: DisputeSwitches.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo; /** Three switches over one sealed type. Add a subtype and see which ones the compiler finds. */ public class DisputeSwitches { sealed interface Dispute permits Opened, EvidenceSent, Won, Lost {} record Opened(String caseId, long amountMinor) implements Dispute {} record EvidenceSent(String caseId) implements Dispute {} record Won(String caseId) implements Dispute {} record Lost(String caseId, long amountMinor) implements Dispute {} // Step 2: add Arbitration to the permits clause, then uncomment this record. // record Arbitration(String caseId, long feeMinor) implements Dispute {} static String label(Dispute d) { return switch (d) { // exhaustive, no default case Opened o -> "opened"; case EvidenceSent e -> "evidence sent"; case Won w -> "won"; case Lost l -> "lost"; }; } static long ledgerImpact(Dispute d) { return switch (d) { // exhaustive, no default case Opened o -> -o.amountMinor(); // money held back while the case runs case EvidenceSent e -> 0; case Won w -> 0; case Lost l -> -l.amountMinor(); }; } static int slaDays(Dispute d) { return switch (d) { case Opened o -> 7; case EvidenceSent e -> 30; default -> 0; // "and anything else": the compiler stops checking }; } public static void main(String[] args) { Dispute[] all = { new Opened("cb_1", 4_200), new EvidenceSent("cb_1"), new Won("cb_1"), new Lost("cb_2", 990) }; for (Dispute d : all) { System.out.printf("%-14s impact %6d sla %2d days%n", label(d), ledgerImpact(d), slaDays(d)); } } }

alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo sealed interface Dispute { data class Opened(val caseId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : Dispute data class EvidenceSent(val caseId: String) : Dispute data class Won(val caseId: String) : Dispute data class Lost(val caseId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : Dispute // Step 2: uncomment this class. Kotlin has no permits clause to edit. // data class Arbitration(val caseId: String, val feeMinor: Long) : Dispute } fun label(d: Dispute): String = when (d) { // exhaustive, no else is Dispute.Opened -> "opened" is Dispute.EvidenceSent -> "evidence sent" is Dispute.Won -> "won" is Dispute.Lost -> "lost" } fun ledgerImpact(d: Dispute): Long = when (d) { // exhaustive, no else is Dispute.Opened -> -d.amountMinor // money held back while the case runs is Dispute.EvidenceSent -> 0 is Dispute.Won -> 0 is Dispute.Lost -> -d.amountMinor } fun slaDays(d: Dispute): Int = when (d) { is Dispute.Opened -> 7 is Dispute.EvidenceSent -> 30 else -> 0 // "and anything else": the compiler stops checking } /** Three whens over one sealed type. Add a subtype and see which ones the compiler finds. */ fun main() { val all = listOf(Dispute.Opened("cb_1", 4_200), Dispute.EvidenceSent("cb_1"), Dispute.Won("cb_1"), Dispute.Lost("cb_2", 990)) for (d in all) { println("%-14s impact %6d sla %2d days".format(label(d), ledgerImpact(d), slaDays(d))) } }

try.expect: javac reports two errors, the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, one in label and one in ledgerImpact. On JDK 27 each also says missing patterns: Arbitration _. slaDays compiles silently and returns 0 for arbitration, which is probably wrong (arbitration has deadlines too), and nothing told you. kotlinc reports the same two functions with Add the 'is Arbitration' branch or an 'else' branch.

refs.title: Preparing for Change: Safe Switching over Sealed APIs (OpenJDK Amber, 2026)

analogy: A sealed type is like the list of settlement currencies in your merchant contract. The contract names them, so finance can write one procedure per currency and know the procedures are complete. Adding a currency means amending the contract, and then every procedure that branches on currency has to be checked, which is exactly what you want. A non-sealed branch is the clause that says "plus any currency a partner bank agrees to handle": you can't list those, but one procedure (send it to the partner) covers them all. The analogy breaks on enforcement: nobody stops a sales rep from quoting a currency that isn't in the contract, while javac and the JVM both refuse a subtype that isn't on the list.
world: Payment services are full of closed lists: payment methods, authorization outcomes, dispute stages, ledger entry kinds, the event types on one Kafka topic. Make each of them a sealed interface of records, and the consumer that handles a topic becomes one switch with no default. The day someone adds RefundReversed to the event schema, the consumer, the projection that builds the read model and the metrics tagging all fail to compile until they handle it. That is better than finding out from a dead-letter queue. Keep each hierarchy in one package: on the class path, which is how Quarkus services usually run, javac won't let you split it.
mistake: The usual mistake is adding default -> throw new IllegalStateException() to a switch over your own sealed type, "to be safe". It feels defensive, but it switches off the one check sealing gives you. When a new subtype arrives, the switch still compiles, the new case goes to the default branch, and you find out at run time, from a failed payment. Leave the default out and let the build fail. Keep default for switches where "everything else" really is one answer.

compare.title: The dispute hierarchy in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Dispute.java
java.html: public sealed interface Dispute permits Opened, EvidenceSent, Won, Lost {} record Opened(String caseId, long amountMinor) implements Dispute {} record EvidenceSent(String caseId) implements Dispute {} record Won(String caseId) implements Dispute {} record Lost(String caseId, long amountMinor) implements Dispute {} static String label(Dispute d) { return switch (d) { // no default case Opened o -> "opened"; case EvidenceSent e -> "evidence sent"; case Won w -> "won"; case Lost l -> "lost"; }; }

kotlin.title: Dispute.kt
kotlin.html: sealed interface Dispute { data class Opened(val caseId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : Dispute data class EvidenceSent(val caseId: String) : Dispute data class Won(val caseId: String) : Dispute data class Lost(val caseId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : Dispute } fun label(d: Dispute): String = when (d) { // no else is Dispute.Opened -> "opened" is Dispute.EvidenceSent -> "evidence sent" is Dispute.Won -> "won" is Dispute.Lost -> "lost" }

compare.note: The idea is the same and so is the bytecode: both compilers write a PermittedSubclasses attribute, so each language sees the other's sealed types as sealed. Three things differ. Java names the subtypes in permits (or infers them from one source file) and makes every subtype choose final, sealed or non-sealed; Kotlin's list is whatever is declared in the same package and module, and subtypes are final unless you open them. Java's location rule is the module, or the package on the class path; Kotlin's is always package and module. And Kotlin has data object for a stateless case, where Java uses a record with no components or an enum.

worked.title: Seal the events a Kafka consumer handles

steps.say: A ledger consumer handles three event types with an instanceof chain. Someone adds a fourth type, Adjusted, to the producer. This compiles with no warning, and the consumer starts throwing on the new events in production.
steps.code: public interface LedgerEvent {} void handle(LedgerEvent e) { if (e instanceof Posted p) post(p); else if (e instanceof Reversed r) reverse(r); else throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown event " + e); // Adjusted lands here }

alt.html: interface LedgerEvent fun handle(e: LedgerEvent) { if (e is Posted) post(e) else if (e is Reversed) reverse(e) else throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown event $e") // Adjusted lands here }

steps.say: Seal the event type and make each event a record in the same package. Records are final, so they need no modifier.
steps.code: // 1. close the list public sealed interface LedgerEvent permits Posted, Reversed, Adjusted {} public record Posted(String entryId, long amountMinor) implements LedgerEvent {} public record Reversed(String entryId, String reason) implements LedgerEvent {} public record Adjusted(String entryId, long deltaMinor) implements LedgerEvent {}

alt.html: // 1. close the list sealed interface LedgerEvent { data class Posted(val entryId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : LedgerEvent data class Reversed(val entryId: String, val reason: String) : LedgerEvent data class Adjusted(val entryId: String, val deltaMinor: Long) : LedgerEvent }

steps.say: Replace the chain with a switch that has no default. The chain could never be checked; the switch is checked on every build, and the else throw disappears because there is no "else" left.
steps.code: // 2. one case per event, no default void handle(LedgerEvent e) { switch (e) { case Posted p -> post(p); case Reversed r -> reverse(r); case Adjusted a -> adjust(a); } }

alt.html: // 2. one branch per event, no else fun handle(e: LedgerEvent) = when (e) { is LedgerEvent.Posted -> post(e) is LedgerEvent.Reversed -> reverse(e) is LedgerEvent.Adjusted -> adjust(e) }

steps.say: A switch statement with patterns must be exhaustive too, so the void version is checked just like the expression. Last, write down why the type is sealed, so the next person knows that adding an event is expected and that consumers must be updated, not given a default.
steps.code: /** * Every event on the ledger topic. Sealed because consumers must handle each one. * New events will be added: expect your switch to stop compiling, and handle the new case. */ public sealed interface LedgerEvent permits Posted, Reversed, Adjusted {} // 3. say why

alt.html: /** * Every event on the ledger topic. Sealed because consumers must handle each one. * New events will be added: expect your when to stop compiling, and handle the new case. */ sealed interface LedgerEvent // 3. say why

lab.title: Seal the payment methods
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail. Two of them run javac inside the test, through javax.tools, against your classes: read the Java source they compile.
In PaymentMethod, seal the interface, seal BankTransfer, and give PartnerMethod the modifier that keeps it open to partners (TODO 1 to 3). Run the tests: four should pass now.
In Settlement, write daysToSettle with one case per type and no default (TODO 4).
Write rail with a single case for all bank transfers (TODO 5). Run until all seven tests pass.
Add record Crypto(String chain) implements PaymentMethod {} to the hierarchy and to permits, then run ./gradlew :modernjava:compileJava. Which lines does javac point at? Remove it again.
hints: Types nested in an interface are implicitly public static. Write permits PaymentMethod.Card, ..., or leave permits out, since every subtype is in this one file.
A sealed sub-interface looks like sealed interface BankTransfer extends PaymentMethod permits Sepa, Swift {}.
sealed or non-sealed modifiers expected means a permitted interface has no modifier; an interface can't be final. Records are final already.
The tests call ToolProvider.getSystemJavaCompiler(). If it returns null, Gradle is running on a JRE: point it at a full JDK.

drill.title: Seal a hierarchy from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a sealed RefundOutcome with three results: Issued(String refundId), Rejected(String reason) and Pending, where Pending is itself sealed, with AwaitingIssuer and AwaitingReview(String queue) below it. Then write label(RefundOutcome) with no default, using one case for everything pending. Java first, then Kotlin.

answer.html: sealed interface RefundOutcome permits Issued, Rejected, Pending {} record Issued(String refundId) implements RefundOutcome {} record Rejected(String reason) implements RefundOutcome {} sealed interface Pending extends RefundOutcome permits AwaitingIssuer, AwaitingReview {} record AwaitingIssuer() implements Pending {} record AwaitingReview(String queue) implements Pending {} static String label(RefundOutcome o) { return switch (o) { case Issued i -> "issued " + i.refundId(); case Rejected r -> "rejected: " + r.reason(); case Pending p -> "pending"; // one case covers the sealed branch }; }

alt.html: sealed interface RefundOutcome { data class Issued(val refundId: String) : RefundOutcome data class Rejected(val reason: String) : RefundOutcome sealed interface Pending : RefundOutcome data object AwaitingIssuer : Pending data class AwaitingReview(val queue: String) : Pending } fun label(o: RefundOutcome): String = when (o) { is RefundOutcome.Issued -> "issued ${o.refundId}" is RefundOutcome.Rejected -> "rejected: ${o.reason}" is RefundOutcome.Pending -> "pending" // one branch covers the sealed branch }

recap: sealed ... permits fixes the list of direct subtypes. javac checks it, and the JVM refuses to load a subclass that isn't on it.
Each permitted subtype is final (records already are), sealed (closed one level down) or non-sealed (open again, and still covered by one case).
A sealed class that isn't abstract is itself a possible value, so its subtypes don't cover it. Make it abstract or an interface.
Java subtypes must share the module, or the package on the class path. Kotlin subtypes must share the package and the module.
A switch over a sealed type with no default is checked: add a subtype and every such switch fails to compile. JDK 27 also lists the missing patterns.
Keep default off the dimension that grows. It hides the new subtype instead of reporting it.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to add default -> throw new IllegalStateException("unknown method") to every switch over your sealed PaymentMethod, "to be safe". Explain, in your own words, what that costs and when a default is the right call.
explain.answer: Over a sealed type, a switch with no default is checked by the compiler: it knows every subtype, and the build fails if a case is missing. That is the main reason to seal the type. Adding a default tells the compiler "anything else goes here", so when someone adds a new payment method, every switch still compiles and the new method throws at run time instead, probably on a real payment. Leave the default out and the build gives you the list of switches to update. A default is right only when "everything else" really has one answer, such as rejecting most event types in a given state. For an open branch, use a non-sealed subtype and one case for it, not a default.

deeper.html:
Sealing is enforced in three places, and it helps to know which one you are looking at.

javac enforces it at compile time, with the errors in this lesson. The JVM enforces it at load time, from the PermittedSubclasses attribute. Compile final class B implements S against an old, unsealed S, then run it next to a newer S that is sealed and doesn't list B, and class loading fails with java.lang.IncompatibleClassChangeError: class B cannot implement sealed interface S. That stops a stray jar from smuggling a subtype into your hierarchy. And reflection reports it: Class.isSealed() and Class.getPermittedSubclasses(), both added with sealed classes, are what the tests in this lesson's lab use.

None of the three stops you from adding a subtype yourself, and that is on purpose. The 2026 Amber guide calls adding a permitted subtype "a permissible and compatible evolution" of a sealed API. Clients compiled against the old list keep loading and running; only their switches change behavior. Recompiled, those switches fail to build. Not recompiled, they meet the new subtype at run time and throw MatchException. The guide calls this how Java balances "safety with resilience": you find out either at build time or loudly at run time, never silently. Lesson 3 runs that experiment, and shows that the same thing happens for an enum constant added after the switch was compiled.

For Kotlin interop, one detail is worth checking in your own build. The PermittedSubclasses attribute only exists in class files for JDK 17 and later, so Java sees a Kotlin sealed type as sealed only when kotlinc targets 17 or higher. With the JDK 21 target the labs use, kotlinc 2.4 writes it, and javac rejects final class Bad implements Status {} against a Kotlin sealed Status with the usual not listed in its 'permits' clause error.
